sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Object storage is a flat-namespace data store where every item is a self-contained "object" — a blob of bytes plus user metadata plus a unique key — accessed over an HTTP REST API (PUT/GET/LIST/DELETE) and scaled to virtually unlimited capacity with eleven-nines durability.

Object storage is the storage layer the public cloud was built on. AWS S3 launched in 2006, and its design reflected a deliberate departure from the file systems and SANs that dominated enterprise data centers: instead of a hierarchy of directories and files, S3 presents a single flat namespace of "buckets," and inside each bucket every object is addressed by an opaque key. There is no `mkdir`, no `readdir`, no POSIX `open()` — every interaction is an HTTP verb against a URL like `https://s3.amazonaws.com/my-bucket/images/cat.jpg`. This sounds limiting, but it is the constraint that makes eleven-nines durability (99.999999999%) and exabyte-scale capacity possible. Netflix stores every original master, every transcoded derivative, and every artwork asset in S3; by 2024 its media bucket held hundreds of petabytes across tens of billions of objects, served by a single REST endpoint, with no operator ever thinking about which disk or which node held a particular file.

The architecture of a production object store is a multi-tenant, eventually-consistent key-value system with strong consistency on reads of the latest write. At the physical layer each object is erasure-coded across N disks and M failure domains (S3 uses 11+9 Reed-Solomon across multiple facilities); a write returns success only after the data has been durably persisted to a quorum of those disks, so a single disk failure, rack failure, or even an entire Availability Zone outage does not lose data. At the logical layer, an index service maps each object key to its physical locations; this index is sharded across many nodes and uses consistent hashing so that adding capacity does not require re-indexing existing data. The HTTP front-end is stateless and horizontally scalable, fronted by a global DNS layer (Route 53, Cloudflare) that routes each request to the closest region; for read-heavy workloads, a CDN like CloudFront sits in front, so the typical GET for a Netflix thumbnail is served from an edge PoP 20ms from the user, never touching the origin bucket at all.

The defining trade-off of object storage is throughput-over-latency and durability-over-mutability. A first-byte S3 GET from the same region takes 20–50ms; the same read against a local NVMe SSD takes 0.1ms. Object storage is also write-once: you cannot edit bytes in the middle of an object, you can only overwrite the whole thing, and overwrites are atomic at the object level but not transactional across multiple objects. There is no `append` operation in the S3 API (it was added in 2016 as a special "appendable object" type, but it is rarely used because it cannot be combined with server-side encryption in the same way). For workloads that need random-access reads and writes — a database, a virtual machine disk, a log being tailed — these constraints make object storage the wrong choice. For workloads that need cheap, durable, virtually unlimited storage of immutable blobs — backups, ML training datasets, container images, static website assets, data lake partitions — it is the only sensible choice.

The real-world example that crystallizes the trade-off is Netflix's asset pipeline. Netflix's original masters (the 4K HDR mezzanine files) are stored in S3 Standard with cross-region replication to a second region; transcoding workers read the master via S3 byte-range GETs (a feature that lets you fetch a 1MB slice of a 100GB object without downloading the whole thing), produce derivative renditions, and write them back to the same bucket under a different key. Each rendition's key encodes its metadata — `movies/StrangerThings/S04/E01/1080p/H264.mp4` — and S3 LIST operations with prefix filters (`LIST ?prefix=movies/StrangerThings/S04/`) provide the "directory" listing even though there is no directory at the storage layer; the prefix is just a string match. The CDN front-end caches hot renditions at the edge, so 95% of viewer requests never reach S3 at all. The total cost is a fraction of what block storage would cost for the same data, and the durability means Netflix never has to worry about losing a master if a transcoding worker's local disk fails.

The cost model also matters. S3 charges ~$0.023/GB-month for Standard storage, ~$0.004/GB-month for Glacier Deep Archive, plus per-request fees and egress charges. Block storage (EBS) is ~$0.10/GB-month and is bound to a single AZ — three times the price, one-third the durability footprint, and you pay for it whether or not you read it. For a Netflix-scale library of 100PB, the difference between S3 Standard and EBS is roughly $770K per month in storage cost alone, before egress. The architectural lesson generalizes: pick object storage by default for anything that is "data at rest" and not actively being computed on, and pick block or file storage only when the access pattern requires it (databases, shared filesystems, OS disks).

### Mermaid Diagram ```mermaid flowchart TD Client[Client / App] -->|HTTPS PUT / GET| API[HTTP Front-end
stateless, autoscaled] API --> Auth[SigV4 Auth + IAM] Auth --> Idx[(Index Service
key -> disk locations)] Idx --> EC1[Erasure-coded disk group 1] Idx --> EC2[Erasure-coded disk group 2] Idx --> EC3[Erasure-coded disk group 3] EC1 -.->|replicated| DR1[Dr Site 1] EC2 -.->|replicated| DR1 EC3 -.->|replicated| DR1 CDN[CloudFront / CDN] -.->|cache GETs| API Client -.->|read hot objects| CDN ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` Client (PUT /movies/Inception.mp4) | v HTTPS + SigV4 +------------+ | HTTP FE | stateless, 1000s of replicas +------------+ | v +------------+ +-------------------+ | Index Svc | -----> | key="movies/..." | | (sharded) | | disks=[d3,d7,d12] | +------------+ | meta: {ct,etag,size} | | +-------------------+ v Erasure code (11+9) across 3 AZs +----+ +----+ +----+ +----+ +----+ | d1 | | d2 | | d3 | | d4 | | d5 | ... (20 disks total) +----+ +----+ +----+ +----+ +----+ | v Cross-region replication -> DR region bucket ``` ### Walkthrough 1. Client signs an HTTP PUT with HMAC-SHA256 (SigV4) so the front-end can authenticate statelessly; the key in the URL becomes the object's identifier. 2. The HTTP front-end consults the index service to choose an erasure-coding placement (which disks, which AZs), streams the bytes, and returns 200 only after a quorum of disks acknowledges persistence. 3. A subsequent GET is routed to the nearest disk holding a fragment, the erasure code reconstructs the object (or fetches a full replica for hot objects), and the CDN caches the response so the next GET for the same key is served from the edge.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
"""
Mini object store: flat namespace, HTTP-style API (PUT / GET / LIST / DELETE),
per-object metadata, and a simple replication-to-secondary mock.
"""
import hashlib, time, json
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class Object:
    key: str
    data: bytes
    metadata: dict
    etag: str
    size: int
    created_at: float

class ObjectStore:
    def __init__(self, name: str):
        self.name = name
        self._objects: dict[str, Object] = {}
        self._replica = None  # secondary store for durability

    def attach_replica(self, other: "ObjectStore"):
        self._replica = other

    def put(self, key: str, data: bytes, metadata: dict | None = None) -> str:
        etag = hashlib.md5(data).hexdigest()
        obj = Object(
            key=key, data=data,
            metadata=metadata or {}, etag=etag,
            size=len(data), created_at=time.time(),
        )
        self._objects[key] = obj            # overwrite = atomic at object level
        if self._replica:
            self._replica.put(key, data, metadata)  # cross-region copy
        return etag

    def get(self, key: str) -> Object:
        if key not in self._objects:
            raise KeyError(f"NoSuchKey: {key}")
        return self._objects[key]

    def list(self, prefix: str = "", limit: int = 100) -> list[str]:
        # "Directories" are emulated with prefix string matching
        keys = sorted(k for k in self._objects if k.startswith(prefix))
        return keys[:limit]

    def delete(self, key: str):
        self._objects.pop(key, None)
        if self._replica:
            self._replica.delete(key)

    def stats(self):
        return {
            "object_count": len(self._objects),
            "total_bytes": sum(o.size for o in self._objects.values()),
        }

if __name__ == "__main__":
    primary = ObjectStore("us-east-1")
    dr      = ObjectStore("us-west-2")
    primary.attach_replica(dr)

    primary.put("movies/Inception/1080p.mp4", b"\x00\x00\x01\x00" * 1024,
                {"codec": "h264", "duration_s": 8880})
    primary.put("movies/Inception/720p.mp4",  b"\x00\x00\x01\x00" * 512,
                {"codec": "h264", "duration_s": 8880})
    primary.put("thumbnails/Inception.jpg",   b"JFIF...")

    print("List 'movies/' ->", primary.list("movies/"))
    obj = primary.get("movies/Inception/1080p.mp4")
    print(f"GET -> etag={obj.etag} size={obj.size}B meta={obj.metadata}")
    print("Primary:", primary.stats())
    print("Replica:", dr.stats())   # cross-region copy present
    primary.delete("thumbnails/Inception.jpg")
    print("After delete, replica keys:", dr.list())
```

quiz.explanation: A flat namespace means there is no parent-child directory tree to traverse, lock, or keep consistent — every object is addressed by a single opaque key, and lookup is a single hash table probe. This eliminates the inode tree, directory locks, and rename coordination that make POSIX filesystems hard to shard.

quiz.question: What is the difference between availability, durability, and consistency as they apply to S3, and why does S3's SLA quote 11 nines for one but not the others?
options: S3 Standard is for hot data — ~$0.023/GB-month, millisecond access, 99.99% availability.
Before December 2020 S3 was only eventually consistent for overwrites and deletes — a PUT followed by a GET could return either the old or the new version, which broke…
Standard S3 permissions cannot enforce this — an admin with s3:DeleteObject can always delete.
Durability is the probability that a byte written will still be retrievable a year later (S3 Standard: 99.999999999% — i.e., you expect to lose 1 object per 10,000,000,000 stored per year).
quiz.explanation: Durability is the probability that a byte written will still be retrievable a year later (S3 Standard: 99.999999999% — i.e., you expect to lose 1 object per 10,000,000,000 stored per year). Availability is the probability that a GET issued right now will succeed (S3 SLA: 99.9%–99.99% depending on tier).

quiz.question: How does S3's erasure coding compare to replication in terms of storage overhead and durability, and why did S3 move from one to the other?
options: Before December 2020 S3 was only eventually consistent for overwrites and deletes — a PUT followed by a GET could return either the old or the new version, which broke…
This is expected behavior, not a bug.
The naive design has three problems.
Replication stores N full copies, so 3x replication costs 3x storage and survives any 2 simultaneous disk failures.
quiz.explanation: Replication stores N full copies, so 3x replication costs 3x storage and survives any 2 simultaneous disk failures. Erasure coding splits an object into k data chunks and m parity chunks, any k of which suffice to reconstruct the object — so 11+9 (k=11, m=9) survives 9 simultaneous failures for 1.82x storage overhead, versus 3x for the same durability with 3x replication.
